questions.q: Match each utility to what it does.
pairs: Scrambles files so they cannot be read without the key
Moves the parts of files together so they are read faster
Makes files smaller so they take less space to store or send
Keeps a second copy of files in case the first is lost
questions.feedback: Four utilities, four different jobs. None of them is part of the operating system's own management work.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.5 Lesson 4 — Utility workshop, station 1: What is utility software?

questions.q: Explain why defragmenting a magnetic hard disk makes it faster to read files, but does nothing for a solid state drive.

markPoints.concept: on a hard disk a fragmented file is spread across the platters
markPoints.exemplar: On a hard disk the parts of a file end up scattered across the platters.

markPoints.concept: so the read/write head has to move further and the read takes longer
markPoints.exemplar: The read/write head has to move further, so reading the file takes longer.

markPoints.concept: a solid state drive has no moving parts, so where the data sits makes no difference
accept: no moving parts|nothing moves|no head|no platter|solid state
markPoints.exemplar: An SSD has no moving parts, so it makes no difference where the data is.

questions.example: On a magnetic hard disk the parts of a file become scattered across the platters, so the read/write head has to move between them and reading the file takes longer. Putting the parts back together means less head movement. A solid state drive has no moving parts at all, so every location takes the same time to reach and defragmenting it achieves nothing — while wearing the drive out slightly.
questions.paraphrase: A file on a magnetic drive gets split across the disc, and because the arm must travel between the pieces, reading it is slower; gathering them together reduces that movement. On a solid state drive nothing moves, so the position of the data is irrelevant.
questions.feedback: Three ideas, and the third is the one that shows you understand why the first two matter.
questions.hint: What physically has to happen on a hard disk that does not happen on an SSD?

questions.q: Explain why encrypting a laptop's hard disk protects the data on it if the laptop is stolen.

markPoints.concept: the data is scrambled so it cannot be read without the key
accept: key|password|passphrase|decrypt|without the key|without a key|without the password|need the key|needs the key
markPoints.exemplar: The data is scrambled and cannot be read without the key.

markPoints.concept: so a thief who takes the disk out still gets nothing useful
accept: thief|thieves|stolen|steal|takes the disk|takes the drive|another computer|different computer|another machine|nothing useful|no use|still cannot|still unreadable
markPoints.exemplar: This means a thief can take the disk out and put it in another computer and still get nothing.

questions.example: Encryption scrambles the contents of the disk so that they are meaningless without the key. A thief can take the drive out and plug it into their own machine, and it will still be unreadable, because the login password is not what is protecting it — the encryption is.
questions.paraphrase: The contents are turned into something unreadable unless the correct key is supplied, so even moving the drive to another machine gives the thief nothing.
questions.feedback: Unreadable without the key, and why moving the disk does not help.

questions.q: Encrypting a file stops it from being deleted.
questions.feedback: Encryption protects what is inside a file, not whether it exists. Deleting an encrypted file is just as easy.

questions.q: Why might a user compress a folder before emailing it?
options: To make it small enough to send and quicker to upload
To stop the recipient from opening it
To make the files inside open faster
To check the files for errors
questions.feedback: Compression reduces size, which is about sending and storing. It does nothing for how fast a file opens afterwards.

questions.q: State one disadvantage of compressing a file.

markPoints.concept: it has to be decompressed before it can be used, which takes time and processing
accept: decompress|uncompress|unzip|extract|expand|open|restore|before it can be used|before you can use|back to normal
markPoints.exemplar: It has to be decompressed before it can be used, which takes time.

questions.example: The file has to be decompressed before it can be used, which takes time and processing — and with lossy compression some of the original data is gone for good.
questions.paraphrase: Extra time and processing are needed to expand it again before it can be opened.
questions.feedback: The cost of getting it back. Losing quality is the other acceptable answer, but only for lossy compression.

questions.q: Match each kind of backup to what it copies.
pairs: Only the files that have changed since the last backup
Whatever is due, at a time nobody has to remember
questions.feedback: A full backup is slow to make and quick to restore. An incremental one is the other way round.

questions.q: Explain one reason a school keeps a backup copy of its data somewhere other than the school building.

markPoints.concept: a fire, flood or theft could destroy everything in one place
markPoints.exemplar: A fire or flood would destroy both the data and a backup kept in the same building.

markPoints.concept: so a copy somewhere else is the only one certain to survive
accept: elsewhere|another site|off site|offsite|cloud|different place|another building|survive|still have|restore|recover
markPoints.exemplar: This means a copy somewhere else is the only one that would survive.

questions.example: A fire, a flood or a burglary would take the servers and any backup sitting beside them in the same cupboard. A copy held off site, or in the cloud, is the only one certain to survive, which is the whole point of keeping it somewhere else.
questions.paraphrase: Since a single disaster at one location would destroy both the original and a copy stored next to it, only a copy held elsewhere is guaranteed to remain.
questions.feedback: What could destroy both copies, and why distance fixes it.
